title: Imports and Setup
content: Imports Mathlib's `Nat.Prime.Basic` for primality predicates (`Nat.Prime`, `Nat.minFac`) and general tactics. The formalization works with $\mathbb{N}$ throughout, using `%` (modular reduction) as the primary operation for residue class membership. No `Set` or `Finset` imports are needed since coverage is expressed via existential quantifiers over primes.
mathContext: Residue classes $a + p\mathbb{Z}$ are represented computationally via `n % p = a % p`. The Chinese Remainder Theorem and Mertens' estimates are axiomatized rather than imported, since Mathlib's CRT is for `ZMod` rather than `Nat.mod`.

title: Residue Assignment
content: Defines a residue assignment as a dependent function mapping each prime $p \leq x$ (with proof of primality and bound) to a natural number $a_p$ representing the chosen residue class. The assignment determines which integers each prime 'covers': $n$ is covered by prime $p$ when $n \equiv a_p \pmod{p}$.
mathContext: A **residue assignment** is a function $\alpha : \{p \leq x : p \text{ prime}\} \to \mathbb{N}$ where $\alpha(p)$ represents the class $\alpha(p) + p\mathbb{Z}$. Each class has density $1/p$ among the integers. For covering congruence systems, the assignment must be chosen so the union of classes $\bigcup_p (\alpha(p) + p\mathbb{Z})$ covers all of $[0, x)$.

title: Prime Partition Structure
content: A `PrimePartition` splits the primes $\leq x$ into two non-empty sets $A$ and $B$ via a Boolean classifier `inA`. The non-emptiness witnesses ensure both parts contain at least one prime. This structure encodes the combinatorial heart of the problem: allocating prime 'resources' between two covering tasks.
mathContext: The partition $\{p \leq x : p \text{ prime}\} = A \sqcup B$ with $A, B \neq \emptyset$. By the prime number theorem, $|\{p \leq x\}| \sim x/\log x$, so the number of possible partitions is $2^{\pi(x)} - 2 \sim 2^{x/\log x}$. The problem asks whether *any* of these (combined with a residue assignment) achieves dual coverage.

title: Coverage by A and B
content: Defines `CoveredByA` and `CoveredByB`: an integer $n$ is covered by set $A$ (resp. $B$) if there exists a prime $p \in A$ (resp. $q \in B$) such that $n \equiv a_p \pmod{p}$ (resp. $n \equiv a_q \pmod{q}$). These are existential propositions — no constructive witness is required.
mathContext: $\text{CoveredByA}(n) \iff n \in \bigcup_{p \in A} (a_p + p\mathbb{Z})$ and $\text{CoveredByB}(n) \iff n \in \bigcup_{q \in B} (a_q + q\mathbb{Z})$. By the **inclusion-exclusion principle**, the probability that a random integer in $[0, \text{lcm})$ is uncovered by $A$ is approximately $\prod_{p \in A} (1 - 1/p)$ when the primes are distinct (CRT independence).

title: Dual Covering
content: A **dual covering** requires every $n < x$ to be covered by *both* $A$ and $B$ simultaneously. This is strictly harder than single coverage: it demands the prime resources be split so that each half independently forms a complete covering system for $[0, x)$.
mathContext: $\text{IsDualCovering}(x, \alpha, A \sqcup B) \iff \forall n < x: n \in \bigcup_{p \in A} (a_p + p\mathbb{Z}) \wedge n \in \bigcup_{q \in B} (a_q + q\mathbb{Z})$. The conjunction makes this a **two-fold covering** requirement. By Mertens, the total 'coverage capacity' $\sum_{p \leq x} 1/p \sim \log\log x$ grows slowly, so splitting it in half is non-trivial.

title: Erdős Problem #467: The Main Conjecture
content: The central open problem: for all sufficiently large $x$, there exist a residue assignment and a prime partition achieving dual coverage. Stated as an axiom since the problem is OPEN. The existential threshold $X$ means the conjecture allows finitely many small exceptions. Erdős and Graham posed this in their 1980 monograph (p. 93).
mathContext: $\exists X \in \mathbb{N}, \forall x \geq X, \exists \alpha, \exists A \sqcup B: \text{IsDualCovering}(x, \alpha, A \sqcup B)$. The original formulation in [ErGr80] has **ambiguous quantifiers** — it is unclear whether the residue assignment $\alpha$ is universal or existential, and whether $A, B$ depend on $x$. The formalization chooses the most natural reading.
relatedConcepts: open problems in combinatorial number theory

title: Basic Properties of Residue Classes
content: Five elementary lemmas: (1) $n \bmod p < p$ for prime $p$, (2) $n \bmod p = 0 \iff p \mid n$, (3) every $n$ is even or odd, (4) residue classes are periodic with period $p$, (5) every $n \geq 2$ has a prime factor, and (6) prime factors of $n$ are $\leq n$. These build the foundation for analyzing which integers a given residue assignment covers.
mathContext: The key structural fact is **periodicity**: if $n \equiv a \pmod{p}$, then $n + kp \equiv a \pmod{p}$ for all $k$. Combined with the fact that every $n \geq 2$ has a prime factor $p \leq n$ (by `Nat.minFac`), this shows the residue class 0 covers all composites. The challenge for dual covering is handling $n = 1$ and distributing prime coverage efficiently.

title: Prime Factor Bounded by x
content: Every $n$ with $2 \leq n < x$ has a prime factor $p \leq x$. This is the key observation that makes single coverage easy: using residue class 0 for every prime, every integer $\geq 2$ is automatically covered by its smallest prime factor. The difficulty of Problem #467 is achieving this with *two disjoint* subsets of primes.
mathContext: If $2 \leq n < x$, then $\text{minFac}(n)$ is prime, divides $n$, and satisfies $\text{minFac}(n) \leq n < x$. Hence $n \in \bigcup_{p \leq x} (0 + p\mathbb{Z})$. This gives single coverage for $[2, x)$ trivially; the problem is that splitting primes into $A$ and $B$ means each half has a sparser sieve.

title: Covering by Zero Residue Classes
content: Three results about using residue class 0 for all primes: (1) $n = 0$ is covered by every prime, (2) $n = 1$ is NOT covered by any prime (since no prime divides 1), and (3) every $n \geq 2$ is covered by its smallest prime factor. The failure at $n = 1$ shows why the zero assignment alone cannot solve the dual covering problem — non-zero residue classes must be used for at least some primes.
mathContext: With assignment $\alpha(p) = 0$ for all $p$: coverage of $n$ requires $p \mid n$. Then $1$ is uncovered since $p \nmid 1$ for all primes $p$. A non-trivial assignment (e.g., $\alpha(2) = 1$) can cover 1 via the class $1 + 2\mathbb{Z}$, but this means 2 no longer covers even numbers via class 0, illustrating the **allocation trade-off**.

title: The Zero Assignment and Its Properties
content: Defines `zeroAssignment`: assign residue class 0 to every prime. The lemma `zero_assign_cover_iff` shows that under this assignment, $n$ is covered by prime $p$ if and only if $p \mid n$. This is the simplest assignment but fails to cover 1. It serves as a baseline for understanding how more sophisticated assignments improve coverage.
mathContext: The **zero assignment** $\alpha \equiv 0$ gives coverage $\{n : p \mid n\} = p\mathbb{Z}$ for each prime $p$. The union $\bigcup_{p \leq x} p\mathbb{Z} = \mathbb{N} \setminus \{1\}$ (all composites and 0, but not 1). For dual covering, we need each half $A$ and $B$ to cover $[0, x)$, which requires assigning at least one small prime in each half a non-zero residue class to capture 1.

title: Partition and Dual Covering Constraints
content: Five structural theorems about dual coverings and partitions: (1-2) a dual covering implies each half $A$ and $B$ independently covers all of $[0, x)$; (3) every $n < x$ is hit by primes from *both* sides; (4) any partition uses at least two distinct primes (one per side); (5) the partition assigns different labels to at least one pair of primes; (6) any partition requires $x \geq 2$. These formalize the minimal structural requirements.
mathContext: The **double hit** property: $\forall n < x, \exists p \in A, q \in B: n \equiv a_p \pmod{p} \wedge n \equiv a_q \pmod{q}$. Since $A \cap B = \emptyset$ and $p \neq q$ is possible but not required (the same prime cannot be in both), every $n$ gets at least two covering witnesses from different primes. The constraint $x \geq 2$ follows from the need for at least one prime in the partition.

title: Residue Class Periodicity and Counting
content: Three lemmas on residue class structure: (1) residue classes are periodic with period $p$: $(n + p) \bmod p = n \bmod p$; (2) in $[0, p)$, each element is its own residue: $a \bmod p = a$ for $a < p$; (3) there are exactly $p$ residue classes mod $p$. These underpin the probabilistic heuristic that each residue class has density $1/p$.
mathContext: The residue classes $\{0, 1, \ldots, p-1\}$ partition $\mathbb{Z}$ into $p$ arithmetic progressions of common difference $p$. Each has **natural density** $1/p$. By the **Chinese Remainder Theorem**, for distinct primes $p_1, \ldots, p_k$, the joint residue classes partition $\mathbb{Z}$ into $\prod p_i$ classes, each of density $1/\prod p_i$.

title: Chinese Remainder Theorem for Distinct Primes
content: Axiomatized CRT: for distinct primes $p \neq q$ and any residues $a, b$, there exists $n$ with $n \equiv a \pmod{p}$ and $n \equiv b \pmod{q}$. This is the foundation for the independence of coverage events. Without CRT, we cannot analyze whether splitting primes yields sufficient coverage in each half.
mathContext: For distinct primes $p, q$: $\forall a, b, \exists n: n \equiv a \pmod{p} \wedge n \equiv b \pmod{q}$. More precisely, $n$ is unique modulo $pq$. This implies that the events '$p$ covers $n$' and '$q$ covers $n$' are **independent** for uniformly random $n \in [0, pq)$. The probability $n$ is uncovered by $\{p, q\}$ is $(1 - 1/p)(1 - 1/q)$.

title: Mertens' Third Theorem (Axiomatized)
content: Axiomatizes Mertens' product estimate: $\prod_{p \leq x} (1 - 1/p) \sim e^{-\gamma}/\log x$ where $\gamma \approx 0.5772$ is the Euler-Mascheroni constant. This controls the probability that a random integer is uncovered by all primes $\leq x$ using residue class 0. For the dual covering problem, each half $A$ and $B$ must have $\prod_{p \in A}(1 - 1/p) \cdot x < 1$ (heuristically) to cover all of $[0, x)$.
mathContext: **Mertens' third theorem** (1874): $\prod_{p \leq x} \left(1 - \frac{1}{p}\right) = \frac{e^{-\gamma}}{\log x}\left(1 + O\left(\frac{1}{\log x}\right)\right)$. For a subset $S$ of primes, the 'uncovered fraction' is $\prod_{p \in S}(1 - 1/p)$. The dual covering requires this to be $< 1/x$ for *both* $A$ and $B$, which by Mertens means each half needs $\sum_{p \in A} 1/p \gg \log\log x$.

title: Problem Summary and Restatement
content: Records the problem status as OPEN and restates the key observation that every $n \geq 2$ has a prime factor. The theorem `coverage_exceeds_target` is a direct corollary of `has_prime_factor`, confirming that single coverage is trivial. The entire difficulty lies in the dual requirement.
mathContext: Single coverage: $\forall n \geq 2, \exists p \text{ prime}: p \mid n$. This trivially gives $[2, x) \subseteq \bigcup_{p \leq x} p\mathbb{Z}$. The gap between single and dual coverage is the essence of Problem #467: passing from $\sum 1/p \sim \log\log x$ (enough for one cover) to needing two independent sub-sums each $\gg \log\log x$.
